title: Observability-driven recovery for tool-call timeouts in streamed envelopes
creator: Luca Martinez
description: Problem statement: When LLM responses emit interleaved structured frames and invoke external tools (function calls) during streaming, transient tool timeouts or partial emissions can leave the client with incomplete objects and no reliable way to recover or reconcile. Current behavior: consumers often receive a partial JSON envelope and a trailing error frame (timeout, 504, tool-unavailable) and must either retry the entire request (expensive) or attempt ad-hoc reconciliation client-side. Goal: define acceptance criteria and a pragmatic design that leverages server-side observability (telemetry, event markers) and lightweight commit semantics in the stream to enable deterministic recovery, safe retries, and actionable operator/engineer debugging info without requiring protocol-level schema changes for most customers.
acceptance_criteria: Stream framing: Every streamed structured emission that can trigger a tool call MUST include a lightweight incremental commit marker frame (commit_id) before the tool invocation frame. Commit markers are opaque strings and are idempotency anchors for downstream reconciliation.

Timeout semantics: If a tool invocation times out (as defined by runtime-configured tool_timeout_ms), the platform must emit a standardized terminal frame (tool_timeout) that contains the commit_id, tool_name, and a short reason code. Clients receiving a tool_timeout must be able to determine whether a retry/resume is safe based solely on commit_id and reason code.

Observability envelope: Each terminal frame emitted on timeout/error MUST be associated with a telemetry event that contains request_id, commit_id, tool_name, model_version, region, and latency_ms. That telemetry must be queryable in the Console within 1 hour of emission and linked from the request trace.

Deterministic replay: Given the same input prompt and commit_id, the runtime MUST be able to replay downstream tool-call side effects idempotently for retriable error classes (timeout, transient network) for at least 5 minutes after the original request, assuming tool backend supports idempotency tokens.

Client guidance: The Console and API docs must provide explicit client-side guidance and example code showing 3 recovery strategies: optimistic resume (if commit_id present), server-driven reroute to fallback model, and full-request retry. Each strategy must include pseudocode and cost/latency tradeoffs.

Backward compatibility: Clients that do not understand commit markers must still be compatible: streams must remain valid JSON or newline-delimited frames; commit marker frames are optional for consumer parsing and should not break existing stream parsers.

Test coverage: End-to-end tests simulating tool timeouts, slow tool responses, and tool misfires must exist in the runtime test harness and be automated in CI with reproducible fixtures. Tests must assert emitted commit_id markers, telemetry events, and client-visible terminal frames.

Console UX: In the request trace view, timeouts must display a dedicated card with commit_id, tool_name, suggested remediation (retry/resume/fallback), and a link to the exact logs (raw frames) for the request. This UI must be available in the staging Console build for validation before GA.

Privacy/security: Telemetry payloads must not include PII or the full tool payload; only metadata (commit_id, truncated tool_name, reason_code, latency). Security review required for the telemetry schema prior to rollout.
out_of_scope: Redesign of function-call protocol or adding new binary transport formats (we will keep existing framing).
Guarantees for non-idempotent tool side effects where tool backend does not accept idempotency tokens (those remain customer responsibility).
Large-scale changes to client SDKs beyond examples and migration notes (full SDK changes to adopt commit markers are follow-up work).
success_metrics: Reduction in customer-reported incidents due to partial streamed tool failures by 40% within 8 weeks of GA.
95% of tool-timeout traces in Console show commit_id and a linked telemetry event within 1 hour.
At least one major enterprise customer adopts optimistic resume strategy and reports measurable token-cost savings vs full-retry in first 30 days.
E2E test coverage: >= 90% pass rate for simulated tool timeout scenarios in CI for the runtime test harness.
test_cases: Simulate tool_timeout: provoke a tool backend that drops connections after N ms and assert the stream contains commit_id and a tool_timeout terminal frame and telemetry event appears in staging Console.
Replay idempotency: issue the same prompt with commit_id and verify side effects are not duplicated when runtime performs a replay within the 5-minute window (mock tool supports idempotency token).
Backward-compat parser: run existing clients that ignore commit frames and validate they can still process the stream (no parse errors).
Console card: create a synthetic trace with a timed-out tool and verify Console displays the timeout card, commit_id, and links to raw frame logs.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (staging): Implement commit_id emission + terminal timeout frames in runtime; wire telemetry to staging Console; run full regression test suite. (2 weeks)
Phase 2 (pilot): Enable for 3 internal teams and 1 pilot customer; collect feedback, iterate on reason codes and Console UX. (2 weeks)
Phase 3 (GA): Flip on by default for hosted API; publish SDK examples and migration guide; monitor telemetry for incidents and rollback toggle. (1 week)
Fallback: Provide a runtime feature flag to disable commit markers per-tenant for 48 hours rollback window.
open_questions: What is the canonical format and entropy length for commit_id to balance collision risk vs payload size?
Should commit_id be issued by the runtime or by the client/SDK when possible? Operational tradeoffs and security considerations need engineering input.
How long should the deterministic replay window be configurable per-tenant? Default proposed: 5 minutes. Engineering to recommend safe default considering cache/KV retention costs.
Do we need a separate error taxonomy (retryable vs non-retryable) for tool failures beyond timeout/network?
